keywords.definition: The processor: the component that carries out instructions by repeatedly fetching, decoding and executing them.
The part of the processor that carries out arithmetic operations (such as addition and subtraction) and logical operations (such as AND, OR and comparisons) on data.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Control Unit: decodes instructions and coordinates the processor; it doesn't do the calculations.

keywords.definition: The part of the processor that decodes instructions and sends control signals to coordinate the other components and the movement of data into, out of and within the processor.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: ALU: performs the arithmetic and logic; the Control Unit directs it.

keywords.definition: A small, very fast storage location inside the processor that holds an instruction, a memory address or an item of data while it is being used.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Cache: also fast memory on the processor, but holds copies of frequently used instructions and data from RAM rather than the value being worked on right now.

keywords.definition: A register that holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: MAR: holds the address of the memory location currently being read from or written to.

keywords.definition: A register that holds the data currently being processed and stores the results of calculations carried out by the ALU.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: MDR: holds data on its way to or from memory; the ACC holds the value being worked on and the ALU's result.

keywords.definition: A register that holds the address of the memory location currently being read from or written to.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: MDR: holds the data or instruction itself, not its address.

keywords.definition: A register that holds the data or instruction that has just been read from memory, or that is about to be written to memory.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: MAR: holds the address of the memory location, not the data stored there.

keywords.definition: A register that holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: PC: holds the address of the next instruction, not the current instruction itself.

keywords.definition: A set of parallel wires that carries signals between the components of a computer, such as between the processor and memory.
A bidirectional bus that carries data and instructions between the processor, memory and input/output devices.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Address bus: carries memory addresses, one way only, from the processor to memory.

keywords.definition: A unidirectional bus that carries memory addresses from the processor to memory; its width determines how many memory locations can be addressed.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Data bus: carries the data and instructions themselves, in both directions.

keywords.definition: A bidirectional bus that carries control signals, such as memory read, memory write and clock signals, between the control unit and the other components.
The cycle the processor repeats for every instruction: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode it to work out what to do, then execute it.
The number of clock cycles the processor carries out per second, measured in hertz (Hz); a higher clock speed means more instructions can be executed each second.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Number of cores: more cores lets more instructions run at the same time; clock speed is how fast each core works through them.

keywords.definition: An independent processing unit within a processor that can fetch, decode and execute instructions on its own.
A small amount of very fast memory in or next to the processor that stores frequently used instructions and data, so they can be accessed more quickly than from RAM.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: RAM: main memory; much larger but slower to access than cache.

keywords.definition: Overlapping the stages of the FDE cycle, so that while one instruction is being executed the next is being decoded and the one after that is being fetched.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Parallel processing: separate cores or processors working at the same time; pipelining overlaps the stages of different instructions within one processor.

keywords.definition: A processor architecture in which instructions and data are stored in the same memory and travel along the same buses, so they can't be fetched at the same time.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Harvard architecture: separate memories and buses for instructions and data.

keywords.definition: A processor architecture with physically separate memories and buses for instructions and data, so an instruction and an item of data can be accessed at the same time.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Von Neumann architecture: one shared memory and set of buses for both.

keywords.definition: Modern processors combine both designs: instructions and data share main memory (Von Neumann), but the processor has separate caches for instructions and for data (Harvard).
A processor design with a large set of complex instructions, some taking several clock cycles, so a task needs fewer lines of assembly code.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: RISC: a small set of simple instructions, each typically taking one clock cycle.

keywords.definition: A processor design with a small set of simple instructions, each typically completed in one clock cycle, which makes pipelining easier.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: CISC: many complex instructions, some taking several clock cycles.

keywords.definition: A processor with a large number of cores designed to carry out the same operation on many items of data at the same time, used for graphics and other highly parallel tasks such as modelling and data mining.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: CPU: fewer, more powerful cores suited to general-purpose and sequential tasks.

keywords.definition: Processing in which one instruction is carried out on many items of data at the same time.
A processor with two or more cores on a single chip, so several instructions, or several programs, can be processed at the same time.
Using two or more processors or cores at the same time to carry out different parts of a task, or different tasks.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Pipelining: overlaps the stages of instructions inside one processor rather than using several processors.

keywords.definition: Hardware used to enter data into a computer system, such as a keyboard, barcode scanner, microphone or sensor.
Hardware used to present the results of processing to a person or another system, such as a monitor, printer, speaker or actuator.
Non-volatile storage that holds programs and data that are not currently in use, such as a hard disk drive, SSD or optical disc.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: RAM: main memory holding what is in use right now, and volatile.

keywords.definition: Storage that records data by magnetising tiny areas of a spinning disk or a tape in one of two directions, such as a hard disk drive or magnetic tape.
Storage that uses a laser to read (and on some discs write) data on the reflective surface of a disc, such as a CD, DVD or Blu-ray.
Solid-state, non-volatile storage that holds data electronically in memory chips with no moving parts, such as an SSD, USB memory stick or SD card.
Volatile main memory that holds the programs and data currently in use, and can be both read from and written to.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: ROM: non-volatile and normally read-only; holds start-up instructions.

keywords.definition: Non-volatile memory whose contents cannot normally be changed, used to store the instructions needed to start the computer, such as the BIOS.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: RAM: volatile, read/write memory for programs and data in use.

keywords.definition: Describes memory that loses its contents when the power is switched off, such as RAM.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Non-volatile: keeps its contents without power.

keywords.definition: Describes memory or storage that keeps its contents when the power is switched off, such as ROM, flash and magnetic storage.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Volatile: loses its contents without power.

keywords.definition: Storage that may appear to be local but is physically located elsewhere on the network, remotely or in the cloud.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Virtual memory (1.2.1): part of secondary storage used as if it were extra RAM when RAM is full.

keywords.definition: System software that manages the computer's hardware and resources and provides a platform and user interface for running other software.
The part of the operating system that allocates memory to processes, keeps them separate from each other, and moves data between RAM and secondary storage when needed.
Dividing memory into fixed-size blocks called pages, so a program's pages can be stored in any free page frames in memory, not necessarily next to each other.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Segmentation: divides memory into variable-size blocks based on the logical parts of a program.

keywords.definition: Dividing memory into variable-size blocks called segments, each holding a logical part of a program such as a subroutine or a data structure.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Paging: fixed-size pages, divided physically rather than by what the program contains.

keywords.definition: An area of secondary storage used as if it were extra RAM when RAM is full; pages not currently needed are swapped out to it and swapped back in when required.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Virtual storage (1.1.3): storage located elsewhere on a network or in the cloud.

keywords.definition: When the computer spends more time swapping pages between RAM and virtual memory than running programs, so it slows down badly.
A signal to the processor from hardware or software saying that something needs attention, which may cause the processor to stop its current task and run an interrupt service routine.
The code that runs to deal with a particular interrupt; afterwards, the saved state of the interrupted task is restored and it carries on.
How the operating system decides which process gets processor time next, so that time is shared fairly and efficiently between processes.
A scheduling algorithm that gives each process a fixed time slice in turn; a process that hasn't finished goes to the back of the queue.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: First come first served: each process runs to completion before the next one starts; no time slices.

keywords.definition: A scheduling algorithm that runs processes in the order they arrive, each one to completion before the next starts.
A scheduling algorithm that uses several queues of different priority, moving processes between queues according to how they behave (for example, how much processor time they use).
A scheduling algorithm that runs the waiting process with the shortest estimated total running time next, letting it run to completion.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Shortest remaining time: can interrupt the running process when a shorter one arrives.

keywords.definition: A scheduling algorithm that always runs the process with the least time left to finish, switching to a newly arrived process if it would finish sooner.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Shortest job first: once a job starts, it runs to completion.

keywords.definition: An operating system that runs across several computers and makes them appear to the user as a single system, sharing tasks and resources between them.
A small operating system built into a dedicated device, such as a washing machine or car engine controller, designed for a specific task with limited resources.
An operating system that appears to run several programs at the same time by switching the processor between them very quickly.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Multi-user operating system: lets several users use the computer's resources at once.

keywords.definition: An operating system that allows several users to use one computer's resources at the same time, using scheduling to share processor time fairly between them.
An operating system that guarantees to process inputs and respond within a fixed, very short time, used where delays could be dangerous, such as in aircraft or medical equipment.
Firmware stored in ROM that runs when the computer is switched on: it checks the hardware (POST), then loads the operating system's boot loader from storage.
Software that lets the operating system communicate with a particular hardware device by translating the operating system's general instructions into ones the device understands.
Software that takes on the function of a machine, for example running an operating system inside another, or executing intermediate code.
Code that is partly translated (such as bytecode) and can be run on any platform that has a suitable virtual machine to execute it.
Software that lets the user carry out a task, such as a word processor, web browser, database or graphics editor.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Utility software: maintains or improves the running of the computer rather than doing the user's task.

keywords.definition: System software that performs a specific task to maintain or improve the running of the computer, such as disk defragmentation, backup, compression or anti-virus.
Software whose source code is made freely available, so users can view, modify and redistribute it under its licence.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Closed source: only the compiled program is supplied and the source code is kept private.

keywords.definition: Software whose source code is kept private by its owner; users get only the compiled program and a licence that restricts how they can use it.
A program that converts source code into machine code: a compiler, an interpreter or an assembler.
A translator that converts the whole of a high-level program into machine code (object code) in one go, producing an executable that can be run without the compiler.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Interpreter: translates and runs the program one line at a time, every time it runs.

keywords.definition: A translator that translates and executes a high-level program one line at a time, stopping at the first error it finds.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Compiler: translates the whole program once and produces an executable file.

keywords.definition: A translator that converts assembly language into machine code, generally one machine code instruction for each assembly language instruction.
A program as written by the programmer in a programming language, before it is translated.
The machine code produced by translating source code, which may still need to be linked with library code before it can run.
Instructions in binary that the processor can execute directly.
The first stage of compilation: comments and whitespace are removed and the source code is split into tokens, with identifiers added to a symbol table.
The smallest meaningful unit of source code, such as a keyword, identifier, operator or value, produced by lexical analysis.
A table built during compilation that records each identifier (such as a variable or subroutine name) with information about it, such as its data type and scope.
The stage of compilation that checks the tokens follow the rules (grammar) of the language, reports any syntax errors, and builds an abstract syntax tree.
A tree representing the structure of the program, built during syntax analysis and passed on to code generation.
The stage of compilation that produces object code (machine code) from the abstract syntax tree.
The stage of compilation that changes the code so it runs faster or uses less memory, without changing what it does, for example by removing redundant instructions.
A collection of pre-written, pre-tested code (such as subroutines) that programmers can use in their own programs.
A program that combines object code with the library code it uses into a single executable file.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Loader: copies the executable into memory so it can run.

keywords.definition: Part of the operating system that copies an executable program (and any dynamically linked libraries it needs) into memory so it can run.
Copying the library code a program needs into its executable file, which makes the file larger but means it runs without the library installed.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Dynamic linking: the library stays separate and is loaded when the program runs.

keywords.definition: Keeping library code in a separate file that is loaded when the program runs, so executables are smaller and many programs can share one copy of the library.
A software development model in which each stage (such as analysis, design, implementation, testing and maintenance) is completed in order before the next one begins.
Approaches to software development that build the software in short, repeated iterations, delivering working parts often and adapting to changing requirements through close contact with the client.
An agile methodology that develops software in short iterations using practices such as pair programming, test-first development and a customer representative working with the team.
An extreme programming practice in which two programmers work at one computer, one writing code while the other reviews it, swapping roles regularly.
A software development model that repeats a cycle of planning, risk analysis, development and evaluation, building a larger version of the software each loop; suited to large, high-risk projects.
A software development model that builds a series of prototypes quickly, getting user feedback on each one, until the prototype becomes the final product.
An early, incomplete version of a system built to show users how it will look and work and to get their feedback.
A sequence of steps that can be followed to solve a problem or complete a task.
A way of writing an algorithm using structured, code-like statements that are not tied to any particular programming language.
A diagram that shows an algorithm using standard symbols (such as start/stop, process, decision and input/output) connected by arrows.
A style or approach to programming, such as procedural, object-oriented or low-level, each suited to different kinds of problem.
A language in which a program is a sequence of instructions grouped into procedures and functions, using sequence, selection and iteration.
A language close to the processor's own instructions, such as machine code or assembly language, giving direct control of the hardware.
A low-level language that uses mnemonics in place of binary machine code instructions, usually with one mnemonic per machine code instruction.
A short, memorable code for a machine code instruction, such as ADD or LDA in assembly language.
A simplified model of a Von Neumann computer with a small instruction set, used to learn assembly language programming.
The part of a machine code or assembly language instruction that says which operation to carry out.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Operand: the data, or the address of the data, the operation works on.

keywords.definition: The part of an instruction that holds the data to be used, or the address of that data.
LMC instruction that adds the value stored at the given memory address to the accumulator.
LMC instruction that subtracts the value stored at the given memory address from the accumulator.
LMC instruction that copies the value in the accumulator into the given memory address.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: LDA: copies a value from memory into the accumulator (the opposite direction).

keywords.definition: LMC instruction that copies the value stored at the given memory address into the accumulator.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: STA: copies the accumulator into memory (the opposite direction).

keywords.definition: LMC instruction that always jumps to the given address, by setting the program counter to it.
LMC instruction that jumps to the given address only if the value in the accumulator is zero.
LMC instruction that jumps to the given address only if the value in the accumulator is zero or positive.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: BRZ: branches only when the accumulator is exactly zero.

keywords.definition: LMC instruction that takes a value from the user and stores it in the accumulator.
LMC instruction that outputs the value in the accumulator.
LMC instruction that stops the program.
LMC instruction that reserves a memory location (labelled) to hold data, optionally with a starting value.
The way an instruction's operand is interpreted to find the data: immediate, direct, indirect or indexed.
An addressing mode in which the operand is the actual value to be used.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Direct addressing: the operand is the address where the value is stored.

keywords.definition: An addressing mode in which the operand is the memory address of the value to be used.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Indirect addressing: the operand is the address of a location holding the address of the value.

keywords.definition: An addressing mode in which the operand is the address of a memory location that holds the address of the value to be used.
An addressing mode in which the address of the value is found by adding the operand to the value in the index register; useful for working through an array.
A register whose value is added to the operand in indexed addressing; incrementing it steps through consecutive memory locations.
A language in which programs are built from objects, created from classes, that combine data (attributes) with the code that acts on it (methods).
A template that defines the attributes and methods that objects of that type will have.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Object: a specific instance created from a class.

keywords.definition: An instance of a class, with its own values for the class's attributes.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Class: the template the object is created from.

keywords.definition: Creating an object from a class, which runs the class's constructor; in OCR pseudocode, for example, myDog = new Dog("Fido", "Scottish Terrier").
A method that runs when an object is created, used to set up its attributes; in OCR pseudocode it is a procedure called new.
A variable that belongs to a class or object and holds data about it.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Method: a subroutine that belongs to the class.

keywords.definition: A subroutine (procedure or function) that belongs to a class and defines a behaviour of its objects.
When a subclass takes on the attributes and methods of its superclass, and can add its own or override them.
A class whose attributes and methods are inherited by one or more subclasses; also called a parent class.
A class that inherits the attributes and methods of a superclass; also called a child class.
Keeping an object's attributes private so they can only be accessed or changed through its public methods, such as get and set methods.
An access level meaning an attribute or method can only be used from inside its own class.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Public: can be used from outside the class.

keywords.definition: An access level meaning an attribute or method can be used from outside its class; in OCR pseudocode, methods and attributes are public unless stated otherwise.
Public methods that return (get) or change (set) the value of a private attribute, so other code can't access the attribute directly.
The ability of objects of different classes to respond to the same method call in their own way, for example a subclass overriding a method it inherits.
A named value that cannot be changed while the program is running.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Variable: a named value that can change while the program runs.

keywords.definition: A named location in memory that holds a value which can change while the program is running.
Reducing the size of a file so it takes up less storage space and can be transferred faster, for example over the Internet.
Compression that permanently removes some data, usually detail people are unlikely to notice, so the original file can't be exactly restored.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Lossless compression: the original can be rebuilt exactly.

keywords.definition: Compression that reduces file size without losing any data, so the original file can be restored exactly.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Lossy compression: some data is removed for good.

keywords.definition: Lossless compression that replaces a run of repeated values with one copy of the value and a count, for example AAAAABB becomes 5A2B.
Lossless compression that replaces repeated entries (such as words or patterns) with a short unique code, storing a dictionary of codes so the file can be rebuilt.
Scrambling data using an algorithm and a key so that it can't be understood by anyone who doesn't have the key to decrypt it.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Hashing: one-way; a hash can't be turned back into the original data.

keywords.definition: Data before it is encrypted, or after it has been decrypted.
Data after it has been encrypted.
Encryption in which the same key is used to encrypt and decrypt, so the key must be shared securely between sender and receiver.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Asymmetric encryption: uses a pair of different keys.

keywords.definition: Encryption that uses a pair of keys: data encrypted with the receiver's public key can only be decrypted with the receiver's private key.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Symmetric encryption: one shared key for both.

keywords.definition: The key in an asymmetric key pair that is shared openly and used by others to encrypt data for the key's owner.
The key in an asymmetric key pair that is kept secret by its owner and used to decrypt data encrypted with the matching public key.
Applying a hash function to data to produce a fixed-size value; it is one-way, so the original data can't be worked out from the hash.
An algorithm that turns input data of any size into a fixed-size value (the hash), always giving the same hash for the same input.
A structured, persistent store of data, organised so that it can be easily searched, sorted and updated.
A database that stores all its data in a single table.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Relational database: data split across linked tables.

keywords.definition: A database that stores data in separate tables, one per entity, linked to each other by primary and foreign keys.
A set of records about one type of entity in a database, arranged in rows (records) and columns (fields).
One row in a database table, holding all the data about one item.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Field: one column, a single item of data in each record.

keywords.definition: One column in a database table, holding a single item of data (an attribute) for each record.
A thing about which data is stored in a database, such as a customer or a product; each entity usually has its own table.
A field (or combination of fields) that uniquely identifies each record in a table.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Foreign key: refers to the primary key of another table.

keywords.definition: A field in one table that is the primary key of another table, used to link the two tables.
A field other than the primary key that is indexed so records can be searched for or sorted by it quickly.
A primary key made up of two or more fields that together uniquely identify each record.
A diagram showing the entities in a database and the relationships between them: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.
A relationship in which each record in one table can link to many records in another and vice versa; it is implemented with a link table between the two.
Organising a relational database into tables in a series of steps (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) to reduce data redundancy and avoid inconsistencies.
A table is in 1NF when every field holds a single (atomic) value, there are no repeating groups of fields, and each record has a unique primary key.
A table is in 2NF when it is in 1NF and has no partial dependencies: every non-key field depends on the whole primary key, not just part of a composite key.
A table is in 3NF when it is in 2NF and has no transitive (non-key) dependencies: every non-key field depends only on the primary key.
Unnecessary repetition of the same data in a database, which wastes space and can lead to inconsistent copies; normalisation removes it.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Redundancy (fault tolerance): deliberately keeping duplicate copies so the system survives a failure.

keywords.definition: A data structure that stores the position of each record by the value of a key field, so records can be found quickly without searching the whole table.
A way of selecting data by filling in a visual grid with the fields, tables, criteria and sort order wanted, instead of writing SQL.
A method of capturing data by scanning printed or handwritten text and converting it into editable text.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: OMR: detects marks in set positions, such as multiple-choice answer sheets, rather than reading text.

keywords.definition: A method of capturing data by detecting marks made in fixed positions on a form, such as a multiple-choice answer sheet or lottery ticket.
A plain text format for exchanging tabular data, with one record per line and fields separated by commas.
A plain text format for exchanging data as attribute-value pairs and arrays, easy for people to read and for programs to parse.
A plain text format for exchanging data in which each item is enclosed in descriptive, user-defined tags.
A standard language used to create, query and change the data in relational databases.
SQL command that returns the chosen fields FROM one or more tables, optionally WHERE a condition is true; SELECTs can be nested.
SQL clause that limits a command to the records meeting a condition, which can combine tests with AND and OR.
SQL operator used in a WHERE clause to match a pattern containing wildcards, for example WHERE Surname LIKE "Sm%".
A character that stands for other characters in SQL: * selects all fields, and % matches any sequence of characters in a LIKE pattern.
SQL clause that combines records from two tables where a field matches, such as a foreign key and the primary key it refers to (an inner join).
SQL command that adds a new record to a table: INSERT INTO table (fields) VALUES (values).
SQL command that removes the records meeting a condition from a table: DELETE FROM table WHERE condition.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: DROP: removes the whole table, not just records.

keywords.definition: SQL command that deletes a whole table (or database), including its structure and all its data: DROP TABLE table.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: DELETE: removes records but keeps the table.

keywords.definition: The rule that every foreign key value must match an existing primary key in the linked table, so there are no references to records that don't exist.
A single logical operation on a database, possibly made up of several steps, that must be completed in full or not at all.
Handling database operations as transactions so the data stays correct even when many users change it at once or a failure happens part-way.
The four properties that make transactions reliable: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability.
The ACID property that a transaction is either completed in full or not at all; a part-finished transaction is rolled back.
The ACID property that a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, never breaking its rules (such as referential integrity).
The ACID property that transactions running at the same time don't affect each other; the result is the same as running them one after another.
The ACID property that once a transaction is completed, its changes are saved permanently and survive a system failure.
Preventing other users from changing a record while one user is updating it, so that one update doesn't overwrite another.
Keeping duplicate copies of data or hardware, often in different places, so the system keeps working and no data is lost if one part fails.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Data redundancy: unwanted repetition of data, removed by normalisation.

keywords.definition: Two or more computers or devices connected together so they can communicate and share resources.
A set of rules that governs how data is transmitted and received between devices, such as its format, addressing and error checking.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Standard: an agreed specification that many manufacturers follow so that different hardware and software work together.

keywords.definition: An agreed specification (for hardware, software or data formats) that manufacturers and developers follow so that products from different companies work together.
Dividing network communication into layers, each with its own protocols that handle one part of the job and only interact with the layers directly above and below.
The set of four protocol layers used on the Internet: application, transport, internet and link.
The top layer of the TCP/IP stack: protocols used by applications to send and receive data, such as HTTP, SMTP and FTP.
The TCP/IP layer that splits data into packets, numbers them, adds port numbers and handles error checking and re-sending of lost packets (TCP).
The TCP/IP layer that adds source and destination IP addresses to each packet and routes packets across networks (IP).
The bottom TCP/IP layer, which sends the data across the physical network between devices on the same network, using their hardware (MAC) addresses.
A unique numerical address that identifies a device on a network, used to route packets to the right destination.
A small unit of data sent across a network, made up of a header (including source and destination addresses and a sequence number), the payload and a trailer for error checking.
A system of servers that translates domain names (as in a URL) into IP addresses.
The full address of a resource on the web, including the protocol and domain name, for example https://www.ocr.org.uk/index.html.
A network covering a small geographical area, such as one building or site, where the organisation usually owns the infrastructure.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: WAN: covers a large area and usually uses infrastructure owned by third parties.

keywords.definition: A network covering a large geographical area, connecting LANs together using third-party infrastructure such as telephone lines or satellites; the Internet is the largest WAN.
Sending data as packets that may each take a different route across the network and are put back in order at the destination.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Circuit switching: a dedicated path is set up for the whole communication.

keywords.definition: Setting up a dedicated communication path between two devices for the whole of a communication, as in a traditional telephone call.
Hardware or software that monitors traffic between networks and blocks packets that don't meet set rules, such as those from blocked IP addresses or ports.
A server that sits between a user's device and the Internet, making requests on the user's behalf; it hides the user's IP address and can filter and cache content.
Software designed to cause harm or gain unauthorised access, such as viruses and spyware.
Malware that attaches itself to other files or programs and spreads when they are run or shared.
Malware that secretly monitors what a user does, such as recording keystrokes, and sends the information to a third party.
An attack that floods a server or network with so many requests that legitimate users can't access it.
An attack in which SQL code is typed into an input box on a website so that the database runs it, for example to reveal or delete data.
Sending fake messages, such as emails that appear to come from a bank, to trick people into giving away personal details like passwords.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Pharming: redirects users to a fake website even when they type the correct address.

keywords.definition: Redirecting users from a genuine website to a fake one, for example by changing DNS records or the hosts file, so they enter their details into it.
Software, such as anti-virus and anti-spyware, that scans for, detects and removes malware.
Hardware that lets a device connect to a network; each NIC has a unique hardware (MAC) address.
A device that connects devices on a LAN and sends each packet only to the device it is addressed to.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Hub: sends every packet to every device.

keywords.definition: A device that connects devices on a LAN and sends every packet it receives to all of them.
A device that forwards packets between different networks, choosing a route towards each packet's destination IP address.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Switch: forwards packets within one network.

keywords.definition: A device that converts digital data into signals that can be carried over a telephone or cable line, and converts them back.
A device that lets wireless devices connect to a wired network.
A network in which central servers provide resources and services (such as files, email or web pages) to client devices that request them.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Peer-to-peer: no central server; every device is equal.

keywords.definition: A network with no central server, in which every device is equal and shares its resources directly with the others.
The markup language that defines the structure and content of a web page using tags.
A language that describes how HTML elements are presented, such as their colour, font and size.
A programming language used to make web pages interactive, usually run in the browser (client side).
A named style, written with a full stop (such as .infoBox), that can be applied to any number of elements using class="infoBox".
keywords.dont_confuse_with: CSS identifier: styles one unique element, written with #.

keywords.definition: A style written with a hash (such as #menu) that applies to the one element with that id, as in id="menu".
CSS written directly in an element's style attribute, such as <h1 style="color:blue;">, affecting only that element.
A separate .css file linked to pages with the <link> tag, so the same styles can be applied across a whole website.
Collecting and storing information about web pages, found by web crawlers, in an index so that search results can be returned quickly.
A program (also called a spider) that visits web pages and follows their links, collecting information about each page for a search engine's index.
An algorithm that ranks web pages by how many pages link to them and how important those linking pages are.
Processing carried out on the user's device, usually by JavaScript in the browser, for example checking a form before it is sent.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Server-side processing: carried out on the web server before the page is sent.

keywords.definition: Processing carried out on the web server, for example in PHP, such as searching a database and building the page that is sent back.
A basic data type built into a programming language: integer, real (floating point), character, string or Boolean.
A data type for whole numbers, positive or negative, with no fractional part.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Real: numbers that can have a fractional part.

keywords.definition: A data type for numbers that can have a fractional part, stored in floating point form; also called float.
A data type for a single letter, digit, symbol or other character from a character set.
A data type for a sequence of characters, such as a name or a sentence.
A data type with only two possible values: true or false.
Converting a value from one data type to another, such as int("3") returning the integer 3 or str(3) returning the string "3".
A base 2 number system that uses only the digits 0 and 1, which computers use to store all data.
The base 10 number system, using the digits 0 to 9; also called decimal.
A single binary digit, 0 or 1; the smallest unit of data.
A group of 4 bits, which can be shown as a single hexadecimal digit.
A group of 8 bits.
The leftmost bit of a binary number, with the largest place value; in signed representations it shows whether the number is negative.
A way of representing signed binary integers in which the most significant bit is the sign (0 positive, 1 negative) and the remaining bits are the size of the number.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Two's complement: the MSB has a negative place value, so arithmetic works normally.

keywords.definition: A way of representing signed binary integers in which the most significant bit has a negative place value (−128 in 8 bits); to negate a number, invert all its bits and add 1.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Sign and magnitude: the MSB is only a sign flag.

keywords.definition: When the result of a calculation is too large to be stored in the number of bits available.
A base 16 number system using the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F (10 to 15); each hex digit represents exactly 4 bits.
A way of representing real numbers in binary as a mantissa and an exponent, where the value is mantissa × 2^exponent.
The part of a floating point number that holds its significant digits, with the binary point after the first (sign) bit; in the exam it is in two's complement.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Exponent: says how far to move the binary point.

keywords.definition: The part of a floating point number that says how many places to move the binary point (right if positive, left if negative); in the exam it is in two's complement.

Adjusting a floating point number so the mantissa has no unnecessary leading digits: it starts 01 for a positive number or 10 for a negative number, giving the maximum precision for the bits available.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Normalisation (databases): organising tables to reduce redundancy; unrelated.

keywords.definition: Moving every bit in a binary number left or right by a number of places, filling the gaps with 0s; a left shift multiplies by 2 per place and a right shift divides by 2 per place (bits shifted off the end are lost).
A binary pattern combined with a value using a bitwise operator to change or test particular bits: AND with 0 clears a bit, OR with 1 sets a bit, and XOR with 1 flips a bit.
A defined list of characters that a computer can represent, each with a unique binary code.

keywords.term: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
keywords.definition: A character set using 7 bits per character, so it represents 128 characters: English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Unicode: many more bits, so it covers every language.

keywords.definition: A character set that uses up to 32 bits per character, so it can represent characters from all the world's writing systems as well as symbols and emoji; its first 128 codes match ASCII.
A static data structure holding a fixed number of items of the same data type under one name, each accessed by its index (starting at 0 in OCR pseudocode).
keywords.dont_confuse_with: List: can change size and can hold items of different types.

keywords.definition: An array with more than one index for each item, such as a 2D array (rows and columns, e.g. board[0,0]) or a 3D array.
A data structure that groups related items of data, called fields, which can be of different data types, under one name.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Array: every item is the same data type.

keywords.definition: A data structure holding an ordered collection of items that can grow or shrink, with items added, removed or changed while the program runs.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Tuple: ordered but can't be changed once created.

keywords.definition: An ordered collection of items that is immutable: once it has been created, its items can't be changed, added or removed.
A data structure whose size is fixed when it is created, such as an array.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Dynamic data structure: can change size while the program runs.

keywords.definition: A data structure that can grow and shrink while the program is running, using memory only as it is needed.
A last in, first out (LIFO) data structure: items are pushed onto and popped off the top only.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Queue: first in, first out; added at the back, removed from the front.

keywords.definition: The rule followed by a stack: the most recently added item is the first to be removed.
Adding an item to the top of a stack (after checking the stack isn't full).
Removing and returning the item at the top of a stack (after checking the stack isn't empty).
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Peek: returns the top item without removing it.

keywords.definition: Returning the item at the top of a stack without removing it.
A first in, first out (FIFO) data structure: items are added (enqueued) at the back and removed (dequeued) from the front.
The rule followed by a queue: the item added earliest is the first to be removed.
Adding an item to the back of a queue (after checking the queue isn't full).
Removing and returning the item at the front of a queue (after checking the queue isn't empty).
A queue stored in a fixed-size array in which the front and rear pointers wrap around to the start when they reach the end, so freed spaces are reused.
A dynamic data structure made of nodes, each holding data and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer gives the first node.
One item in a linked list, tree or graph, holding data and links (pointers or edges) to other items.
A value that holds the address or index of another item, such as the next node in a linked list.
A data structure made of nodes (vertices) connected by edges, used to represent networks such as roads or social connections.
A connection between two nodes in a graph or tree; also called an arc.
A graph whose edges have a direction, so they can only be followed one way.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Undirected graph: edges can be followed both ways.

keywords.definition: A graph whose edges have no direction, so each can be followed both ways.
A graph in which each edge has a value (weight), such as a distance, time or cost.
A 2D array showing which nodes of a graph are connected, with a row and column for each node (holding the weight, or 1, where an edge exists).
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Adjacency list: stores only each node's neighbours.

keywords.definition: A way of storing a graph in which each node has a list of the nodes it is connected to (and the edge weights).
A data structure of nodes connected by edges in a hierarchy, with one root node at the top and no cycles; each node except the root has exactly one parent.
The node at the top of a tree, which has no parent.
A node in a tree that has no children.
A tree in which each node has at most two children, a left child and a right child.
A binary tree in which every node's left subtree holds smaller values and its right subtree holds larger values, so it can be searched quickly.
A data structure that stores each item at a position worked out by applying a hash function to its key, so items can be found in a single step if there are no collisions.
When a hash function gives the same position for two different keys; handled, for example, by placing the item in the next free position (linear probing) or chaining items together in a list.
The Boolean operation that is true only when both inputs are true; written A ∧ B.
The Boolean operation that is true when at least one input is true; written A ∨ B.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: XOR: true when exactly one input is true, not both.

keywords.definition: The Boolean operation that reverses its input, so true becomes false and false becomes true; written ¬A.
The Boolean operation that is true when exactly one of its two inputs is true; written A ⊻ B.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: OR: also true when both inputs are true.

keywords.definition: The Boolean relation that is true when both sides have the same value; written ≡ (↔ is also accepted).
A table showing the output of a logic circuit or Boolean expression for every combination of inputs (2^n rows for n inputs).
An electronic component that performs a Boolean operation, such as AND, OR, NOT or XOR, on one or more inputs.
A grid of a Boolean expression's outputs, with inputs labelled in Gray code order (00, 01, 11, 10), used to simplify the expression by grouping adjacent 1s.
Rules for negating a combined expression: ¬(A ∧ B) ≡ ¬A ∨ ¬B, and ¬(A ∨ B) ≡ ¬A ∧ ¬B (break the bar, change the sign).
The Boolean rule A ∧ (B ∨ C) ≡ (A ∧ B) ∨ (A ∧ C), and likewise A ∨ (B ∧ C) ≡ (A ∨ B) ∧ (A ∨ C).
The Boolean rule that brackets can be regrouped when the same operator is used throughout: (A ∧ B) ∧ C ≡ A ∧ (B ∧ C), and the same for ∨.
The Boolean rule that the order of inputs to ∧ or ∨ doesn't matter: A ∧ B ≡ B ∧ A, and A ∨ B ≡ B ∨ A.
The Boolean rule that negating twice gives the original value: ¬¬A ≡ A.
A logic circuit that stores one bit: on the rising edge of the clock pulse its output takes the value of its data input, and it holds that value until the next clock pulse.
A logic circuit that adds two bits, giving a sum (A XOR B) and a carry (A AND B).
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Full adder: also adds a carry in, so adders can be chained.

keywords.definition: A logic circuit that adds two bits and a carry in, giving a sum and a carry out; full adders can be chained to add binary numbers of any length.
The law that controls how organisations collect, store and use personal data, through eight principles, and gives individuals rights over data held about them.
Data about a living person who can be identified from it, such as their name, address or medical records.
The living person whom personal data is about.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Data controller: the organisation that decides how the data is used.

keywords.definition: The person or organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed, and is responsible for following the Data Protection Act.
A request from a data subject to see the personal data an organisation holds about them, which the organisation must answer.
The law that makes it illegal to access computer material without authorisation, to do so intending to commit further offences, or to make unauthorised changes to computer material.
Using a computer system or its data without permission, for example by guessing someone's password; an offence under the Computer Misuse Act.
The law that protects the creators of original work, including software, from having it copied, distributed or adapted without permission, and protects inventions through patents.
The legal right of the creator of an original work, such as software, music or text, to control how it is copied and distributed; it applies automatically.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Patent: protects an invention or new process and must be applied for.

keywords.definition: A legal right, which must be applied for, that stops others making, using or selling a new invention for a set period.
The law that allows authorised public bodies, such as the police and security services, to intercept and monitor communications and require access to encrypted data.
An issue about what an individual believes is right or wrong.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Ethical (social) issue: what society as a whole considers right or wrong.

keywords.definition: An issue about what society as a whole considers right or wrong, and about the effects on society; the OCR guide pairs ethical with social.
An issue about how technology affects, or is affected by, the beliefs, customs, languages and practices of different groups of people.
Using computers and machines to carry out tasks that were previously done by people.
Decisions made by a computer system from data and set rules or models, without a person making each decision, such as approving loans or flagging fraud.
The ability of a computer system to carry out tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as recognising speech, making decisions or learning from data.
Discarded electronic devices, which contain toxic materials and valuable metals and must be recycled or disposed of safely.
Controlling or blocking what information people can access or publish, for example a government or organisation filtering websites.
Monitoring people's behaviour, for example with CCTV, by tracking phone calls and GPS location, or by monitoring emails and Internet use.
Illegally copying or distributing copyrighted material, such as software, films or music.
Messages or content that are abusive, threatening or grossly offensive, such as online harassment or trolling.
The meanings and associations colours carry, which differ between cultures; for example, red can mean danger in one culture and luck in another.
Removing unnecessary details from a problem so that you can focus on the parts that matter for solving it.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Decomposition: breaking a problem into smaller parts, rather than leaving details out.

keywords.definition: A simplified representation of a real situation that keeps only the features needed for the problem, such as a map of a train network that shows stations and connections but not distances.
A condition that must be true before an algorithm or subroutine is run for it to work correctly, such as a list being sorted before a binary search.
Storing data or instructions that have been used, or are likely to be needed, somewhere faster to access, so they don't have to be fetched or worked out again.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Cache (1.1.1): the fast memory in the processor; caching is the general technique, used in hardware and software.

keywords.definition: A self-contained piece of code, such as a subroutine, class or library, that can be used again in other parts of a program or in other programs.
Breaking a problem down into smaller sub-problems that are easier to understand and solve, until each can be solved directly.
A diagram showing how a problem or program is broken down into smaller parts (sub-procedures), drawn as a hierarchy from top to bottom.
A point in an algorithm where a condition is tested and the result decides which path the program takes next.
A Boolean expression, such as x > 5 AND flag == false, that evaluates to true or false and controls a decision or loop.
Carrying out more than one task during the same period of time, with each task starting before the previous one has finished, either by switching between them or by running them in parallel.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Parallel processing: tasks running at exactly the same moment on separate processors or cores.

keywords.definition: Instructions carried out one after another, in the order they are written.
A programming construct that chooses which instructions to run depending on whether a condition is true, using if/elseif/else or switch/case; also called branching.
A programming construct that repeats a block of instructions, either a set number of times or until a condition is met.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Recursion: a subroutine calling itself, rather than a loop.

keywords.definition: A loop that repeats a set number of times, such as for i=0 to 7 ... next i.
A loop that repeats while (or until) a condition is true, such as while ... endwhile or do ... until.
A table used to follow an algorithm by hand, recording the value of each variable (and any output) as each line runs.
When a subroutine calls itself, with each call working on a smaller version of the problem until a base case is reached.
The stopping condition in a recursive subroutine: the case that returns a result without making another recursive call.
An error when the call stack runs out of memory, for example because a recursive subroutine calls itself too many times or never reaches its base case.
A variable declared in the main program (with global in OCR pseudocode) that can be accessed and changed from anywhere in the program.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Local variable: only exists inside its subroutine.

keywords.definition: A variable declared inside a subroutine that only exists, and can only be used, while that subroutine is running.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Global variable: accessible from anywhere in the program.

keywords.definition: The part of a program in which a variable can be accessed.
Writing a program as separate, self-contained modules (such as subroutines), each doing one task, that can be written and tested independently.
A named block of code that carries out a specific task and can be called from elsewhere in the program; either a function or a procedure.
A subroutine that returns a value to the code that called it.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Procedure: carries out a task but doesn't return a value.

keywords.definition: A subroutine that carries out a task but doesn't return a value.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Function: returns a value.

keywords.definition: A variable listed in a subroutine's definition that receives a value (argument) passed in when the subroutine is called.
Passing a copy of the argument's value to a subroutine, so changes made to the parameter don't affect the original variable.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Passing by reference: the subroutine can change the original variable.

keywords.definition: Passing the address of the argument to a subroutine, so changes made to the parameter also change the original variable.
Software that provides tools for writing, running and debugging programs in one place, such as an editor, error reporting, breakpoints and variable watches.
A point set in an IDE where the program pauses when it runs, so the programmer can inspect variable values at that moment.
Running a program one line at a time in an IDE, to see exactly which lines run and how values change.
An IDE tool that shows the value of chosen variables as the program runs, to help find where a value goes wrong.
An error where code breaks the rules (grammar) of the language, so it can't be translated, such as a misspelt keyword or missing bracket.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Logic error: the program runs but gives the wrong result.

keywords.definition: An error in a program's design that lets it run but makes it produce the wrong result, such as using < instead of <=.
A problem that can be solved by an algorithm in a finite number of steps; in practice it also needs to be solvable in a reasonable time with the resources available.
Identifying, from a description of a scenario, what the actual problem is and what needs to be solved.
Solving a problem by repeatedly splitting it into smaller sub-problems of the same type, solving those, and combining the results, as in binary search and merge sort.
Solving a problem by trying a path step by step and, when a path fails, going back to the last decision point to try a different option.
Searching through large amounts of data to find patterns, relationships and trends that weren't previously known.
A rule-of-thumb approach that finds a good enough solution quickly when finding the perfect one would take too long, such as the estimate used in the A* algorithm.
Using mathematical models or simulations to predict how a system will perform (for example, under heavy load) without having to test the real system.
Splitting a task into stages where the output of one stage is the input to the next, so different stages can work on different items at the same time.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Pipelining (1.1.1): the processor overlapping fetch, decode and execute; the same idea applied to hardware.

keywords.definition: Presenting data or a problem visually, such as in a graph or diagram, to make patterns easier to see or to build a mental model of how a program will work.
A way of describing how an algorithm's time or memory requirement grows as the size of its input (n) grows, keeping only the fastest-growing term and ignoring constants.
How the number of steps an algorithm takes grows as the size of its input grows.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Space complexity: how the memory needed grows.

keywords.definition: How the amount of memory an algorithm needs grows as the size of its input grows.
O(1): the time taken stays the same however large the input is, such as accessing an array item by its index.
O(n): the time taken grows in direct proportion to the size of the input, such as a linear search.
O(n^k), such as O(n²): the time taken grows in proportion to the input size raised to a fixed power, such as a bubble sort.
O(2^n): the time taken doubles with each extra item of input, so it becomes impractical even for fairly small inputs.
O(log n): the time taken grows very slowly, increasing by a constant amount each time the input doubles, such as a binary search.
The least time or memory an algorithm can need for an input of a given size, such as finding the target at the first position checked.
The time or memory an algorithm needs on typical inputs of a given size.
The most time or memory an algorithm can need for an input of a given size, such as a bubble sort on data in reverse order.
A search that checks each item in turn from the start until the target is found or the end is reached; works on unsorted data.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Binary search: needs sorted data, and halves the search area each step.

keywords.definition: A search on sorted data that checks the middle item and discards the half that can't contain the target, repeating until the target is found or nothing is left.
A sort that repeatedly passes through the list comparing adjacent items and swapping them if they are in the wrong order, until a pass makes no swaps.
A sort that builds a sorted section at the start of the list, taking each next item and inserting it into its correct position in that section.
A divide and conquer sort that repeatedly splits the list in half until each part has one item, then merges the parts back together in order.
A divide and conquer sort that picks a pivot, moves smaller items before it and larger items after it, then sorts each side in the same way.
The item chosen in quick sort to split the list: smaller items go before it and larger items after it.

An algorithm that finds the shortest path from a start node to every other node in a weighted graph, by repeatedly visiting the unvisited node with the smallest known distance and updating its neighbours' distances.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: A*: aims for one goal node and uses a heuristic to guide the search.

keywords.definition: A shortest path algorithm that finds a route to one goal node by always exploring the node with the lowest cost so far plus a heuristic estimate of the distance left to the goal.
Visiting every node in a tree or graph exactly once, in a set order.
A traversal that goes as far down one branch as possible before backtracking to explore the next, using recursion or a stack.
keywords.dont_confuse_with: Breadth-first: visits all nodes on one level before the next level.

keywords.definition: A depth-first tree traversal that visits a node's left subtree, then its right subtree, then the node itself.
A traversal that visits the start node, then all its neighbours, then their neighbours and so on, level by level, using a queue.
